Industry News: Transformers v5: Simple model definitions powering the AI ecosystem

📅 01 Dec 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020.
  • It has been revealed that today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯.
  • The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Transformers' version v4.0.0rc-1, the initial release candidate for version 4, was released on November 19th, 2020. Five years later, we now release v5.0.0rc-0.

It has been revealed that today, as we launch v5, Transformers is installed more than 3 million times each day via pip - up from 20,000/day in v4 🤯. Altogether, it has now surpassed 1.2 billion installs!

The ecosystem has expanded from 40 model architectures in v4 to over 400 today, and the community has contributed more than 750,000 model checkpoints on the Hub compatible with Transformers, up from roughly 1,000 at the time of v4.

This growth is powered by the evolution of the field and the now mainstream access to AI. As a leading model-definition library in the ecosystem, we need to continuously evolve and adapt the library to continue being relevant. Reinvention is key for longevity in AI.

We’re fortunate to collaborate with many libraries and apps built on transformers, in no specific order: llama.cpp, MLX, onnxruntime, Jan, LMStudio, vLLM, SGLang, Unsloth, LlamaFactory, dLLM, MaxText, TensorRT, Argmax, among many other friends.

For v5, we wanted to work on several notable aspects: simplicity, training, inference, and production. We detail the work that went into them in this post.

Sources indicate that the first focus of the team was on simplicity. Working on transformers, we see the code as the product. We want our model integrations to be clean, so that the ecosystem may depend on our model definitions and understand what’s really happening under the hood, how models differ from each other, and the key features of each fresh model. Simplicity results in wider standardization, generality, and wider support.

Transformers is the backbone of hundreds of thousands of projects, Unsloth included. We build on Transformers to help people fine-tune and train models efficiently, whether that’s BERT, text-to-speech (TTS), or others; to run fast inference for reinforcement learning (RL) even when models aren’t yet supported in other libraries. We're excited for Transformers v5 and are super happy to be working with the Hugging Face team!

According to recent reports, transformers, at the core, remains a model architecture toolkit. We aim to have all recent architectures and to be the “source of truth” for model definitions. We’ve been adding between 1 - 3 upcoming models every week for 5 years, shown in the timeline below:.

We’ve worked on improving that model-addition process.

Recent findings suggest that over the past year, we’ve heavily pushed our modular design as a significant step forward. This allows for easier maintenance, faster integration, and better collaboration across the community.

We give a deeper overview in our Maintain the Unmaintainable blog post. For brevity, we aim to achieve a much easier model contribution process, as well as a lower maintenance burden. One metric we can highlight is that the number of lines of code to contribute (and review), drop significantly when modular is used:.

While we respect the “One model, one file” philosophy, we continue introducing some abstractions making the management of common helpers simpler. The prime example of this is the introduction of the AttentionInterface, which offers a centralized abstraction for attention methods. The eager method will remain in the modeling file; others, such as FA1/2/3, FlexAttention, or SDPA, are moved to the interface.

Over the past couple of years, the increasing amount of 0-day support for fresh model architectures and standardization of attention handling has helped to simplify our support for post-training modern LLMs.

According to recent reports, we’re building tooling to help us identify which existing model architecture a newly introduced model resembles. This feature uses machine learning to find code similarities between independent modeling files. Going further, we aim to automate the conversion process by opening a draft PR for the model to be integrated into our transformers format. This process reduces manual effort and ensures consistency.

Industry observers note that we’ve significantly refactored the modeling and tokenization files. Modeling files have been greatly improved thanks to the modular approach mentioned above, on top of standardization across models. Standardization contributes to abstracting most of the tools that don’t make up a model, so that the modeling code only contains the relevant parts for a model’s forward/backward passes.

Alongside this work, we’re simplifying the tokenization and processing files: going forward, we’ll only focus on the tokenizers backend, removing the concept of “Fast” and “Slow” tokenizers.

We'll use tokenizers as our main tokenization backend, just as we do for PyTorch-based models. We’ll offer alternatives for Sentencepiece or MistralCommon backed tokenizers, which will be non-default but will be supported. Image processors will now only exist with their fast variant, which depends on the torchvision backend.

Finally, we’re sunsetting our Flax/TensorFlow support in favor of focusing on PyTorch as the sole backend; however, we're also working with partners in the Jax ecosystem to ensure we have compatibility between our models and this ecosystem.

With its v5 release, transformers is going all in on PyTorch. Transformers acts as a source of truth and foundation for modeling across the field; we've been working with the team to ensure good performance across the stack.

We're excited to continue pushing for this in the future across training, inference, and deployment.

In a recent development, -- Matt White, Executive Director, PyTorch Foundation. GM of AI, Linux Foundation.

Training remains a significant focus of the team as we head into v5: whereas previously we would focus heavily on fine-tuning rather than pre-training/full-training at scale, we’ve recently done significant work to improve our support for the latter as well.

Supporting pre-training meant reworking the initialization of our models, ensuring that they worked at scale with different parallelism paradigms, and shipping support for optimized kernels for both the forward and backward passes.

Going forward, we’re excited to have extended compatibility with torchtitan, megatron, nanotron, as well as any other pre-training tool that is interested in collaborating with us.

In a recent development, we continue collaborating closely with all fine-tuning tools in the Python ecosystem. We aim to continue providing model implementations compatible with Unsloth, Axolotl, LlamaFactory, TRL and others in the PyTorch ecosystem; but we are also working with tools such as MaxText, in the JAX ecosystem, to have good interoperability between their frameworks and transformers.

All fine-tuning and post-training tools can now rely on transformers for model definitions; further enabling Agentic use-cases through OpenEnv or the Prime Environment Hub.

We’re putting a significant focus on inference for v5, with several paradigm changes: the introduction of specialized kernels, cleaner defaults, new APIs, support for optimized inference engines.

Recent findings suggest that similarly to training, we’ve been putting some effort in packaging kernels so that they’re automatically used in case your hardware and software permits it. If you haven’t heard of kernels before, we recommend taking a look at this doc.

Alongside this effort, we ship two new APIs dedicated to inference:.

According to recent reports, we see this as a major step forward for use-cases such as evaluation, where a great number of inference requests are done simultaneously. We don’t aim to do specialized optimizations like the dedicated inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT LLM). Instead, we aim to be perfectly inter-compatible with these, as detailed in the next section.

The Transformers backend in vLLM has been very enabling to get more architectures, like BERT and other encoders, available to more consumers. We've been working with the Transformers team to ensure many models are available across modalities with the best performance possible. This is just the start of our collaboration: we're happy to see the Transformers team will have this as a focus going into version 5.

-- Simon Mo, Harry Mellor at vLLM.

Industry observers note that standardization is key to accelerating AI innovation. Transformers v5 empowers the SGLang team to spend less time on model reimplementation and more time on kernel optimization. We look forward to building a more efficient and unified AI ecosystem together!

Recent findings suggest that recently, we've been working hand in hand with the most popular inference engines for them to use transformers as a backend. The value added is significant: as soon as a model is added to transformers, it becomes available in these inference engines, while taking advantage of the strengths each engine provides: inference optimizations, specialized kernels, dynamic batching, etc.

We've also been working very closely with ONNXRuntime, llama.cpp and MLX so that the implementations between transformers and these modeling libraries have great interoperability. For example, thanks to a significant community effort, it's now very easy to load GGUF files in transformers for further fine-tuning. Conversely, transformers models can be easily converted to GGUF files for use with llama.cpp.

According to recent reports, the Transformers framework is the go-to place for reference AI model implementations. The framework plays a crucial role in enabling modern AI across the entire stack. The team and the community behind the project truly understand and embrace the spirit of the open-source development and collaboration.

The same is true for MLX, where the transformers' safetensors files are directly compatible with MLX's models.

Industry observers note that it’s hard to overstate the importance of Transformers (and datasets, tokenizers, etc) to the open-source and overall AI ecosystem. I can’t count the number of times I’ve personally used Transformers as a source-of-truth.

In a recent development, finally, we’re pushing the boundaries of local inference and are working hand-in-hand with the executorch team to get the transformers models to be available on-device. We’re expanding the coverage to multimodal models (vision, audio) through optimum.

Recent findings suggest that quantization is quickly emerging as the standard for state-of-the-art model development. Many SOTA models are now released in low-precision formats such as 8-bit and 4-bit (e.g., gpt-oss, Kimi-K2, Deepseek-r1), hardware is increasingly optimized for low-precision workloads, and the community is actively sharing high-quality quantized checkpoints. In v5, we're making quantization a central focus of Transformers support, ensuring full compatibility with all major features, and delivering a reliable framework for training and inference.

We introduce a significant change to the way we load weights in our models; and with this, we move to quantization being a first-class citizen.

Our collaboration with the Transformers team was highly productive, marked by their proactive code reviews, feedback, and technical expertise. Their support was crucial in integrating TorchAO, expanding quantization features, and improving documentation for broader adoption in the V5.

We're excited that v5 has made quantization a first-class citizen. It provides the foundation for bitsandbytes to better support key features like TP and MoEs, and also makes it easier to integrate latest quantization methods.

-- Matthew Douglas & Titus von Koeller, bitsandbytes.

Recent findings suggest that the overarching theme of this version 5 release is “interoperability”. All refactors, performance improvements, and standardization are aligned with this theme. v5 plays nicely and end-to-end with the growing ecosystem: train a model with Unsloth/Axolotl/LlamaFactory/MaxText deploy it with vLLM/SGLang, and export it to llama.cpp/executorch/MLX to run locally!

Sources indicate that version 5 is undeniably an accomplishment of the past five years by a very large number of people in our community. We also see it as a promise, and as a beacon of the direction we want to go.

It has been revealed that we took it as an opportunity to clean up the toolkit and isolate what mattered; we now have a clean slate on top of which to build. Thanks to the many changes from the community and team, improvements in performance, usability, and readability, will be simpler to ship.

Now that v5.0.0's first RC is out there, we'll be eagerly awaiting your feedback. Please check our release notes for all the technical details, and we'll be awaiting your feedback in our GitHub problems!

AI video generators can now turn a prompt or a character image into a few seconds of animation, and anime is one of the most popular styles people ask for. But anime is also one of the hardest styles to get right: flat colors, thin linework and stylized motion expose the weaknesses of video models swiftly. For developers and designers, the useful question is not which tool is “best”, but what each one actually offers, what it cannot do yet, and how to fit it into a real production workflow.

This article compares five generators on what their own pages state, covers the problems they all share, asks whether AI anime videos are worth making, and then explains how the models work and how designers and developers can build a practical workflow, including ffmpeg and API-integration examples. “Best” here depends on the job: the tools are listed in no ranking order, each is linked once to its official site for reference, and the comparison is based on public vendor pages reviewed in November 2026. Features, models and pricing change often, so verify current details before relying on any of them.

We reviewed each vendor’s own site and compared what it states on the same points. This is a documentation-based comparison, not a lab benchmark. Where a page does not state something, we say so instead of guessing.

On its main site, Pollo describes generating video from text prompts or uploaded images and editing existing videos, such as adding, changing, removing or restyling content. It also offers AI image generation, so a character image and the animation can be made in one place.

Strengths for anime work: text-to-video and image-to-video in the same tool, plus video editing and restyling, which suits experimenting with looks.

Limitations and gaps: the pages we could read do not name the underlying models, list credit amounts or pricing, or describe anime-specific controls such as reference characters or first and last frame inputs. You will need to test consistency yourself.

It depends on the job and on what you compare them with. Against a full studio production they are limited. Against having no animation at all, they change what a small team or solo creator can attempt.

Treat the generator as a fast prototyping and shot-making assistant, not a replacement for writing, direction and design. Audience reaction also varies, and some viewers are openly critical of AI-made work, so quality and disclosure both matter.

Industry observers note that most current generators are diffusion models extended to video. As in image diffusion, the model starts from random noise and removes it step by step, guided by your inputs. The extension to video, described in research such as Video Diffusion Models, is that the model denoises a whole sequence of frames together, so that motion and appearance stay coherent over time. Many systems work in a compressed latent space rather than on raw pixels to keep generation affordable.

In a recent development, create an original character sheet with front, side and three-quarter views, a fixed color palette and a clear silhouette. Keep it simple: fewer fine details means less flicker.

Break the sequence into short shots with one action and one camera move each. A four-shot, twenty-second sequence is more realistic than one long generation.

Start each shot from a clean keyframe of your character. Where a tool supports first and last frames or reference images, use them to define the pose and keep identity stable.

Describe subject, action, camera and mood, and add a style anchor. For example: “The girl slowly turns toward the camera, wind moves her hair, petals drift past, gentle push-in, 2D cel shading, clean linework.”.

Scrub through each clip for warped hands, drifting faces and flickering lines. Discard or regenerate failures instead of hoping nobody notices.

Join the best takes, color-match them, add sound and captions, and add disclosure where a platform requires it.

Developers can make the pipeline repeatable. Two patterns help: scripted post-processing with ffmpeg, and a resilient job-based client for any generation API.

The script below extracts a last frame to seed the next shot, normalizes clips to a common size and frame rate so they can be joined, concatenates them, and optionally holds each frame twice for an “on twos” look. Adjust sizes and frame rates to your project.

Video generation is usually asynchronous: you submit a job, then poll or receive a callback. The sketch below shows the pattern with a timeout and backoff. The endpoints and fields are placeholders, so follow your provider’s documentation for real ones.

In a recent development, most are diffusion models for video. They start from noise and remove it step by step across a sequence of frames, guided by a text prompt and often a starting image or reference images, until coherent motion appears.

Usually, for consistency. The image locks the character and style, while the prompt only needs to describe motion.

Thin lines and flat color regions make small frame-to-frame changes visible. Simpler designs, slower motion and post-processing reduce it.

AI anime video generators are useful, but uneven. The five tools reviewed here differ in input modes, consistency tools, developer access and how much their own pages say, and none removes the core problems of consistency, flicker and limited acting. The practical approach is to test several tools on the same shots, keep your workflow tool-agnostic, design characters that are simple and consistent, and review every clip before it ships. Used that way, they are a capable prototyping and shot-making aid, not a substitute for design and direction.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • We gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a newly introduced tool called Hugging Face Skills.
  • Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks.
  • Recent findings suggest that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We gave Claude the ability to fine-tune language models using a newly introduced tool called Hugging Face Skills. Not just write training scripts, but to actually submit jobs to cloud GPUs, monitor progress, and push finished models to the Hugging Face Hub. This tutorial indicates you how it works and how to use it yourself.

Claude Code can use "skills"—packaged instructions, scripts, and domain knowledge—to accomplish specialized tasks. The hf-llm-trainer skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about training: which GPU to pick for your model size, how to configure Hub authentication, when to use LoRA versus full fine-tuning, and how to handle the dozens of other decisions that go into a successful training run.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:.

Recent findings suggest that the model trains on Hugging Face GPUs while you do other things. When it's done, your fine-tuned model appears on the Hub, ready to use.

It has been revealed that this isn't a toy demo. The skill supports the same training methods used in production: supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. You can train models from 0.5B to 70B parameters, convert them to GGUF for local deployment, and run multi-stage pipelines that combine different techniques.

Hugging Face skills are compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI. With integrations on the way for Cursor, Windsurf, and Continue.

This repo includes gemini-extension.json to integrate with the Gemini CLI.

You have to authenticate to your Hugging Face account with a write-access token so that the job can create a model repo.

Configure Hugging Face MCP Server to use your write token by sending it in either the HF_TOKEN or Authorization: Bearer HTTP Headers.

For Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http hf-skills https://huggingface.co/mcp?bouquet=skills --header "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN".

Let's walk through a complete example. We'll fine-tune a small model to see the full workflow, then explore more advanced capabilities.

Start with a simple and clear instruction to fine tune a specific model.

The coding agent analyzes your request and prepares a training configuration. For a 0.6B model on a demo dataset, it selects t4-small—enough GPU for this model size and the cheapest option available.

The open-r1/codeforces-cots dataset is a dataset of codeforces problems and solutions. It is a good dataset for instruction tuning a model to solve hard coding problems.

Recent findings suggest that this works for vision language models too! You can simply run "Fine-tune Qwen/Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct on llava-instruct-mix".

Before your coding agent submits anything, you'll see the configuration:.

This is your chance to adjust anything. Change the output repo name, pick different hardware, or ask Claude to modify training parameters. Once you approve, the agent submits the job.

For example, you can ask the agent to try a test run:.

After submission, you get job details:.

The skill includes Trackio integration, so you can watch training loss decrease in real-time. Jobs run asynchronously so you can close your terminal and come back later. When you want an update:.

Then the agent fetches the logs and summarizes progress.

When training completes, your model is on the Hub:.

That's the full loop. You described what you wanted in plain English, and the agent handled GPU selection, script generation, job submission, authentication, and persistence. The whole thing cost about thirty cents.

The skill supports three training approaches. Understanding when to use each one helps you get better results.

Sources indicate that SFT is where most projects start. You provide demonstration data—examples of inputs and desired outputs—and training adjusts the model to match those patterns.

Recent findings suggest that use SFT when you have high-quality examples of the behavior you want. Customer support conversations, code generation pairs, domain-specific Q&A—anything where you can show the model what good looks like.

The agent validates the dataset, selects hardware (a10g-large with LoRA for a 7B model), and configures training with checkpoints and monitoring.

For models larger than 3B parameters, the agent automatically uses LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) to reduce memory requirements. This makes training 7B or 13B models feasible on single GPUs while preserving most of the quality of full fine-tuning.

DPO trains on preference pairs—responses where one is "chosen" and another is "rejected." This aligns model outputs with human preferences, typically after an initial SFT stage.

Sources indicate that use DPO when you have preference annotations from human labelers or automated comparisons. DPO optimizes directly for the preferred response without needing a separate reward model.

It has been revealed that DPO is sensitive to dataset format. It requires columns named exactly chosen and rejected, or a prompt column with the input. The agent validates this first and shows you how to map columns if your dataset uses different names.

Industry observers note that you can run DPO using Skills on vision language models too! Try it out with openbmb/RLAIF-V-Dataset. Claude will apply minor modifications but will succeed in training.

GRPO is a reinforcement learning task that is proven to be effective on verifiable tasks like solving math problems, writing code, or any task with a programmatic success criterion.

The model generates responses, receives rewards based on correctness, and learns from the outcomes. This is more complex than SFT or DPO, but the configuration is similar.

The agent selects hardware based on your model size, but understanding the tradeoffs helps you make better decisions.

In a recent development, for tiny models under 1B parameters, t4-small works well. These models train rapidly—expect $1-2 for a full run. This is perfect for educational or experimental runs.

For small models (1-3B), step up to t4-medium or a10g-small. Training takes a few hours and costs $5-15.

Sources indicate that for medium models (3-7B), you need a10g-large or a100-large with LoRA. Full fine-tuning doesn't fit, but LoRA makes these very trainable. Budget $15-40 for production.

For large models (7B+), this HF skills job is not suitable.

When testing a workflow, start small:.

The coding agent configures minimal training—enough to verify your pipeline works without real cost.

Always run a demo before committing to a multi-hour production job. A $0.50 demo that catches a format error saves a $30 failed run.

Dataset format is the most common source of training failures. The agent can validate datasets before you spend GPU time.

The agent runs a quick inspection on CPU (fractions of a penny) and reports:.

If your dataset needs transformation, the agent can show you how:.

The agent provides mapping code and can incorporate it directly into your training script.

Recent findings suggest that real-time monitoring helps you catch problems early. The skill configures Trackio by default—after submitting a job, you can watch metrics at:.

In a recent development, this shows training loss, learning rate, and validation metrics. A healthy run shows steadily decreasing loss.

Ask the agent about status anytime:.

Sources indicate that if something goes wrong, the agent helps diagnose. Out of memory? the agent suggests reducing batch size or upgrading hardware. Dataset error? The agent identifies the mismatch. Timeout? The agent recommends longer duration or faster training settings.

After training, you might want to run your model locally. The GGUF format works with llama.cpp and dependent tools like LM Studio, Ollama, etc.

The agent submits a conversion job that merges LoRA adapters, converts to GGUF, applies quantization, and pushes to Hub.

We've shown that coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini CLI can handle the full lifecycle of model fine-tuning: validating data, selecting hardware, generating scripts, submitting jobs, monitoring progress, and converting outputs. This turns what used to be a specialized skill into something you can do through conversation.

The skill is open source. You can extend it, customize it for your workflows, or use it as a starting point for other training scenarios.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that deepMath is an aligned math reasoning agent built on Qwen3-4B Thinking and fine-tuned with GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). Instead of verbose text, the model emits tiny Python snippets for intermediate steps, runs them in a secure sandbox, and folds the results back into its reasoning, reducing errors and output length. The agent is implemented using the smolagents library.

We evaluate DeepMath on four math datasets: MATH500, AIME, HMMT, and HLE, and show that:.

🤖 The math agent alone reduces output lengths by up to 66%, while often improving accuracy.

⚡ GRPO training improves the agent performance even further, in almost all benchmarks.

👉 Code and evaluation scripts: https://github.com/IntelLabs/DeepMath 👉 Model: https://huggingface.co/Intel/deepmath-v1.

It has been revealed that large language models (LLMs) have advanced reasoning capabilities, but mathematical problem-solving remains challenging; chain-of-thought traces can be lengthy and prone to arithmetic mistakes. Recent works[^1][^2] demonstrate that small models can reach strong performance, and other studies[^3] investigate tool use to improve reliability. What those papers generally do not emphasize is reducing trace verbosity or explicitly training models to prefer short, computation-oriented traces executed in a constrained, auditable environment.

Offload deterministic computation to a safe executor.

Train models to prefer concise, computation-oriented traces over verbose text.

In a recent development, deepMath tackles this by combining a small Python executor with a fine-tuned LLM, enabling concise, computation-driven reasoning. The model learns to generate short Python snippets, which are executed in a sandbox and reintegrated into the context. GRPO fine-tuning encourages this behavior by rewarding correctness and encouraging shorter outputs.

Figure 1: The vLLM client and server were modified to use the DeepMath agent in generating the candidates, while using the vLLM backend.

Agent Interface: During inference, the model can output normal tokens or special agent calls containing Python snippets.

Execution: Snippets run in a sandboxed environment with strict safety constraints (no file I/O, no network, timeouts).

Concision: Replace multi-line textual calculations with short, focused snippets.

Determinism & Safety: Enforce strict execution limits.

Interpretability: Snippets are readable and auditable.

Figure 2: Output example where python code is generated, evaluated and the answer is inserted into the trace and used for context.

We fine-tune the model using GRPO, a reward-based optimization that balances:.

Accuracy Reward: +1 for correct answers.

Using code snippets: +1 for generating code snippets, weighted 10:1 vs. the accuracy reward.

Length reduction: shorter lengths are encouraged by limiting the GRPO completion candidates to 5k tokens.

In a recent development, temperature Scheduling: We implemented linear temperature scheduling (T=1.2 → T=0.7) to balance exploration and stability during training. This approach aims to enhance experimentation during the initial training phases, subsequently reducing the temperature as we refine our proficiency in the skill.

In-context Learning: we include 4 solved examples where the trace contains agent calls and executor outputs, so the model learns the syntax and the call/response pattern.

Industry observers note that dataset: we used the Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) subset of the OpenMathReasoning dataset. Note that GRPO only uses the problem, not the solution in the data. This dataset was chosen to ensure the problems benefit from the external tool.

According to recent reports, we benchmarked DeepMath against baselines on four datasets. Metrics include:.

majority@16: robustness across samples, as used in previous math reasoning works, see references.

We compare a baseline configuration (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, no agenting) with our DeepMath model. As ablation, we evaluate the agentic framework we developed running with the untrained Qwen3 model, denoted by +Agent. Additionally, we examine whether the GRPO training (for agentic use) improves non-agentic inference, denoted by +GRPO. Thus the two ablations are independent, not additive.

Industry observers note that we observe the agentic inference reduces output lengths, with mixed accuracy results. The DeepMath model is both GRPO-trained and run in agentic mode, and demonstrates the highest accuracy with shortened traces. We conclude both GRPO training and agentic inference are needed for best results.

Key Insight: DeepMath reduces output length by up to 66% while improving accuracy on challenging datasets.

Accuracy: Offloading computation reduces arithmetic errors.

Efficiency: Shorter outputs mean faster inference and easier interpretability.

Safety: Sandbox execution mitigates risks of running arbitrary code.

Industry observers note that deepMath demonstrates a practical and lightweight way to combine a small executor with an LLM and to train the model to prefer short, computation-driven traces. Offloading deterministic computation reduces arithmetic and numerical errors and shortens traces, and GRPO fine-tuning further encourages concise, correct answers. The result is a more accurate and more interpretable math-solving agent without requiring a massive model or heavyweight external tools.

Recent findings suggest that check out the GitHub repo and share your feedback! Contributions welcome. 🚀.

If you use DeepMath in your research, please cite:.

Scope: we focused on a small model and on mathematical reasoning.

Not long ago, a synthetic voice was easy to spot: flat, rushed and strangely stressed. Today, the best AI text to speech tools can read a script with natural pacing, switch accents, whisper or laugh on cue, and even speak in a voice cloned from a short recording. That makes them useful far beyond screen readers. Developers use them for product voice prompts, marketers for video voiceovers, teachers for course narration and writers for listening back to their own drafts.

This guide explains how modern text-to-speech works, what to look for when choosing a tool, and compares six options: OpenArt, ElevenLabs, Murf AI, Speechify, WellSaid Labs and Amazon Polly. Each section covers strengths, limits and the best use case. The details come from each vendor’s own pages at the time of writing, and plans, models and prices change often, so confirm current terms before you commit.

Sources indicate that openArt’s AI text to speech tool lives inside a wider creative platform. You open the Audio tab, choose Create voice-over, select a model, paste your script, pick a voice, generate, listen and download. It runs in the browser with nothing to install. According to OpenArt’s page, you can switch between models for each script, including Fish Audio Drama 3, Eleven v4 and Eleven v4 Turbo.

Sources indicate that the direction system is what makes it practical for storytelling. You add notes in square brackets, such as [whispering], [laughs] or [pause], directly in the script. OpenArt notes Fish Audio Drama 3 gives close control over single words and mid-line changes of mood, while Eleven v4 reads the whole script to infer the emotion of each line and keeps the voice steady when you regenerate a line. Preset voices are labeled by accent, gender and age, and you can upload a recording of your own voice to clone it.

Because OpenArt also makes video and background music, you can build the voiceover, visuals and soundtrack in one place. It describes a Director mode for planning stories up to five minutes, and the voiceover can also be added in any video editor.

Pricing: Fresh accounts get 40 free credits. Paid prepares add monthly credits and watermark-free downloads, and commercial rights apply on eligible paid plans. Check the pricing page for current plans.

Best for: creators who want expressive voiceovers together with AI video and music.

Recent findings suggest that elevenLabs is one of the best-known names in AI voice. Its text to speech page describes a large voice library, voice design and both instant and professional voice cloning, with the latest model, Eleven v4, positioned as the most expressive. It also lists Eleven v3, Multilingual v2 and a low-latency Flash and Turbo family aimed at real-time use, and it claims support for more than 90 languages and accents, with the exact count varying by model.

For developers, there is a text to speech API with SDKs, which makes it practical for apps, games, agents and automated pipelines. The free strategy includes 10,000 credits a month, and paid prepares start with Starter at $6 a month, then Creator at $22 and Pro at $99, according to the vendor page, with introductory offers on the first month.

In a recent development, pricing: Free plan with 10,000 credits a month. Paid plans from $6 a month as listed on the vendor page.

Best for: expressive narration, multilingual content and apps that need a voice API.

Murf AI positions itself as a studio for voiceovers. Its page lists more than 200 voices, built with permission and partnership from professional voice actors who earn royalties, and support for 35 or more languages for text to speech, with dubbing in 40 or more. The Studio editor offers pitch, speed and intonation controls and a custom pronunciation library, which helps with brand names and technical terms.

Sources indicate that murf also has an API. Its page describes Falcon 2 for conversational use with time-to-first-audio under 100 milliseconds, priced at $0.01 per minute, and Gen 2 for controllable voiceovers. Gen 2’s “Say it My Way” feature lets you record your own rendition so the model reflects your tone and inflections.

It has been revealed that pricing: Free plan with limits. Paid plan prices are on Murf’s pricing page.

Best for: marketing videos, training and presentations where you want to fine-tune delivery.

Speechify is built around reading aloud. You paste text or upload a PDF, DOCX, TXT or EPUB file, pick a voice, adjust playback speed and listen or download the audio. Its page lists more than 1,000 voices across 60 or more languages, including several regional English accents, and the tool works in the browser and in apps for iOS, Android, Mac and Windows, plus Chrome and Edge extensions.

The use cases lean toward productivity and accessibility: studying, going through emails and documents, language learning and support for people with visual impairments, dyslexia or ADHD. A free account saves your documents and syncs them across devices.

Pricing: You can start free. Paid plans are listed on Speechify’s pricing page.

Best for: students, professionals and anyone who wants to listen to documents and articles.

WellSaid Labs focuses on professional voiceover for businesses. Every voice is built from recordings of a real voice actor who consented and is paid when the voice is used, and the voices are licensed for commercial use. Its page describes hundreds of voices across languages, accents, tones and styles.

Pronunciation control is a highlight. You can highlight a word to see suggested pronunciations and save your choice to a team library that applies to every project, and set pacing, emphasis and pronunciation line by line. WellSaid also describes a Producer product that connects AI assistants to WellSaid through MCP and its API.

Pricing: Contact sales for a quote based on your voiceover volume.

Best for: corporate training, product marketing, courses and advertising where licensing and consistency matter.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Polly is Amazon Web Services’ text to speech service, and it is aimed squarely at developers. According to AWS, it supports more than 40 languages and language variants with over 100 male and female voices, and it works through APIs in your code. It supports SSML, the W3C standard markup for phrasing, emphasis and intonation, and custom lexicons that fix the pronunciation of acronyms and terms. Output formats include MP3 and OGG.

Pricing is usage-based. AWS lists a free tier for new accounts, with usage allowances that depend on the voice engine, so estimate your character volume before you decide. A short example shows how little code a basic request takes:.

The sample uses the AWS SDK for JavaScript, calls the neural engine and sends SSML so that the pause and emphasis are explicit. Adjust the region, voice and engine to match what your account supports.

Pricing: Usage-based with a free tier for newly introduced accounts. See the AWS pricing page for current rates.

Best for: apps, IVR systems, notifications and any product that needs automated speech at scale.

Industry observers note that treat this table as a starting point. Features and limits change often, so test two or three tools with the same script.

Modern text-to-speech systems turn written words into audio through several stages.

Newer expressive systems go further by reading the whole script to infer emotion and context, and by accepting direction in the text itself, such as a bracketed note that says to whisper. That is why a single script can produce very different reads depending on the model and the instructions.

If you use a tool with SSML support, you can make a spoken code or number far clearer:.

The say-as element tells the engine to read the number digit by digit, and the break and emphasis tags shape the rhythm. Supported tags and attributes differ between engines, so check the documentation for yours.

What is the best AI text to speech tool? It depends on the job. OpenArt suits voiceovers with video and music, ElevenLabs suits expressive multilingual audio, Murf AI suits studio-style control, Speechify suits listening, WellSaid Labs suits licensed corporate work and Amazon Polly suits developers.

Is AI text to speech free? Several tools offer free plans or credits, but limits are common. Examples include OpenArt’s free credits for new accounts, ElevenLabs’ free monthly credits and Murf’s limited free strategy, which has no commercial licence.

In a recent development, can I use AI voices commercially? Often yes on paid intends, but the rules differ by tool. Always check the current licence before publishing.

Can AI text to speech clone my voice? Some tools support it, including OpenArt and ElevenLabs, usually from a short recording of your own voice. Only clone voices you have permission to use.

It has been revealed that what is SSML? Speech Synthesis Markup Language is a W3C standard that lets you control pauses, emphasis, pronunciation and pitch in synthetic speech. Amazon Polly is one service that supports it.

Which tool is best for developers? Amazon Polly and ElevenLabs both offer APIs, and Murf describes API options as well. Evaluate latency, languages, pricing and SDK support for your use case.

Industry observers note that how do I make AI voices sound less robotic? Write conversationally, add pauses and emphasis, correct pronunciations and split long scripts into short sections. Choose a model that is designed for expressive reads.

AI text to speech is now good enough for real projects, but the right tool depends on what you are making. OpenArt is a strong first stop for expressive voiceovers alongside video and music, ElevenLabs offers a deep voice library and API, Murf AI and WellSaid Labs suit polished, controlled narration, Speechify turns documents into audio and Amazon Polly fits straight into developer workflows. Test two or three with your own script, check the licence and always listen to the full result before it goes live.

In a recent development, every developer has shipped the other kind of page: a lovingly written article or landing page that peaks on launch day and then quietly rots. Screenshots age, statistics expire, rankings slide. Data-driven pages play the opposite game. Built from a living dataset, they republish themselves daily, grow to thousands of URLs, and answer questions nobody had asked when the site introduced. This guide breaks down how they work, using a real fan-run stats site as the running example: one public dataset in, more than ten thousand fresh pages out.

Static pages lose ground because the web moves and they do not. Facts expire, competitors publish fresher answers, and search engines reward pages whose information matches today. A page that cannot enhancement itself must be rewritten by hand, so most sites update a few pages and abandon the rest.

Freshness is not one rule for the whole web; it depends on the query. Nobody needs a CSS tutorial rewritten weekly, but statistics, prices, availability and anything with a season attached decays on a schedule. Developers misjudge this constantly, treating every page like documentation when half their catalogue is really a perishable good. Serve a three-month-old stat as if it were current and readers learn the most damaging lesson a site can teach: do not trust the numbers here.

Then there is the maintenance maths. A hundred hand-written pages each needing one review a year is a hundred small debts, and the interest compounds as the catalogue grows. The team updates the flagship pages, promises to return for the rest, and quietly never does. Data-driven architecture is really a staffing decision disguised as a technical one: humans design the system once, and the system does the updating forever.

A data-driven site has three layers: a dataset that refreshes on a schedule, templates that turn records into pages, and URL patterns that map every meaningful combination owners might search for. Change the data and every page changes; improve a template and ten thousand pages improve at once.

It has been revealed that the running example makes this concrete. A fan-built Overwatch stats tracker republishes Blizzard's public hero data on a daily cycle. From that one feed it generates hero profiles, head-to-head matchup pages and multi-condition tier lists: 10,291 URLs in its sitemap, across six languages, with matchup pages alone accounting for 8,586 of them. Nobody wrote those pages. Somebody designed the system that writes them, which is a very different, and much more scalable, job.

Recent findings suggest that the example runs on Next.js behind a CDN, but the stack is the least important layer of the three. The same pipeline feeding WordPress, Astro or a static site generator would look identical from the reader's side of the glass. Choose boring technology you already know, and spend your originality budget on the dataset and the templates, because that is where readers will feel the difference.

Generated pages stay useful when every URL must earn its existence with data. Set minimum thresholds before a page is published, give each template unique modules its siblings do not have, and noindex combinations with nothing to say. The line between a resource and spam is not automation; it is emptiness.

It has been revealed that quality gates work best when they are public and mechanical. The example site publishes its tier formula openly: 70% of the score from win rate, 30% from pick rate, and a hard floor that excludes heroes picked in under 0.5% of matches from topping the ranking, because a tiny sample cannot prove anything. That single floor is editorial policy expressed as code. Your version might be a minimum number of data points, a minimum price history, or a minimum review count — the number matters less than the fact that the gate exists and applies to every page equally.

Industry observers note that each template also needs modules its siblings cannot copy. A hero profile carries a seven-day trend and its best and worst matchups; a matchup page carries the head-to-head history; a tier list carries the movement since yesterday. Add a short human layer on top — a methodology page explaining the scoring, changelogs narrating what moved — and the catalogue stops reading as output and starts reading as a publication. Google's scaled-content rules target pages manufactured to manipulate rankings with little value; a page that answers a real query with real, current data is the opposite of that. The honest test for any generated URL is simple: if it vanished tonight, would a searcher lose an answer?

It has been revealed that start embarrassingly small: one dataset, one entity type, one template. A football club's results archive, a property portal's sold prices, your own product catalogue — anything structured and refreshed beats a grand plan. Prove one template earns traffic, then add combinations, languages and dashboards in that order.

What is programmatic SEO? Programmatic SEO means generating many pages from a structured dataset using templates, instead of writing each page by hand. Done well, each page answers a distinct search with real data. Done badly, it produces thousands of near-identical pages, which is where its reputation suffers.

In a recent development, is programmatic SEO against Google's rules? No. Google's spam policies target scaled content created mainly to manipulate rankings, with little or no value for customers. Pages generated from real data that answer real queries are publishing. The deciding question is whether a page helps its reader, not how it was produced.

Sources indicate that how often should the data behind pages refresh? Match the refresh to how fast the underlying facts change. Sports and game statistics justify daily pulls, prices often need hourly checks, and reference data may only move monthly. Refreshing faster than reality changes wastes crawl budget and makes 'updated' stamps meaningless.

Do generated pages need unique written text? They need unique value, which is not the same thing. Identical paragraphs on ten thousand pages add nothing, but unique data, comparisons and trends are content in their own right. Add short human-written context per template, and let the data carry the differences between pages.

How many pages should a first project launch with? Launch with the smallest set that proves the template: one entity type, a few hundred pages at most. Validate that search engines index them and users engage before adding combinations and languages. Scaling an unproven template just manufactures tomorrow's cleanup job at industrial size.

In a recent development, the sites quietly winning the long game are not publishing more; they are publishing systems. One honest dataset, one well-built template and strict quality gates will outlast a hundred hand-written pages competing on freshness alone. Try it this week: take one dataset you already own, design a single template with four real modules, and ship fifty pages. Watch what the data does next.

llama.cpp server now ships with router mode, which lets you dynamically load, unload, and switch between multiple models without restarting.

Reminder: llama.cpp server is a lightweight, OpenAI-compatible HTTP server for running LLMs locally.

This feature was a popular request to bring Ollama-style model management to llama.cpp. It uses a multi-process architecture where each model runs in its own process, so if one model crashes, others remain unaffected.

Start the server in router mode by not specifying a model:.

Industry observers note that this auto-discovers models from your llama.cpp cache (LLAMA_CACHE or ~/.cache/llama.cpp). If you've previously downloaded models via llama-server -hf user/model, they'll be available automatically.

In a recent development, on the first request, the server automatically loads the model into memory (loading time depends on model size). Subsequent requests to the same model are instant since it's already loaded.

Returns all discovered models with their status (loaded, loading, or unloaded).

All model instances inherit settings from the router:.

All loaded models will use 8192 context and full GPU offload. You can also define per-model settings using presets:.

The built-in web UI also supports model switching. Just select a model from the dropdown and it loads automatically.

We hope this feature makes it easier to A/B test different model versions, run multi-tenant deployments, or simply switch models during development without restarting the server.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI agents are rapidly becoming essential for building intelligent applications, but creating robust, adaptable agents that scale across domains remains a challenge. Many existing frameworks struggle with brittleness, tool misuse, and failures when faced with complex workflows.

CUGA (Configurable Generalist Agent) was designed to overcome these limitations. It's an open-source, AI Agent that combines flexibility, reliability, and ease of use for enterprise use cases. By abstracting orchestration complexity, CUGA empowers developers to focus on domain requirements rather than the internals of agent building. And now, with its integration into 🚀Hugging Face Spaces🚀, experimenting with CUGA and open models has never been easier.

Recent findings suggest that CUGA is a configurable, general-purpose AI agent that supports complex, multi-step tasks across web and API environments. It has achieved state-of-the-art performance on leading benchmarks:.

🥇 #1 on AppWorld - a benchmark with 750 real-world tasks across 457 APIs.

🥈 Top-tier on WebArena (#1 from 02/25 - 09/25) - showcases CUGA Computer Use capabilities with a complex benchmark for autonomous web agents across application domains.

We're also continuing to innovate with new experimental capabilities, including:.

Figure 1: CUGA Agentic Architecture.

The CUGA architecture begins with the user's message flowing into a chat layer that interprets intent and constructs the user's goal, based on context. A task planning and control component then decomposes this goal into structured subtasks, tracked programmatically through a dynamic task ledger. This ledger supports re-planning when needed, ensuring robust execution. Subtasks are delegated to specialized agents, such as the API agent, which uses an inner reasoning loop to generate pseudo-code instructions before invoking code in a secure sandbox. The system leverages a tool registry that goes beyond MCP protocols to parse and understand tool capabilities, enabling precise orchestration. Once all steps are completed, the final response is returned to the user, delivering reliable, policy-aligned outcomes.

CUGA works best when inference is fast. When each call takes seconds, delays compound and force a tradeoff between agent capability and user experience. Running on high-performance inference platforms like Groq reveals how fast inference fundamentally expands what agent architectures can achieve.

CUGA is fully open source, under the Apache 2.0 license, and you can find us at cuga.dev.

By embracing open models, CUGA aligns with the Hugging Face ethos of democratizing AI-giving developers the freedom to choose models that best fit their needs, whether for experimentation or production.

CUGA has been tested with a variety of open models, including gpt-oss-120b and Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct-fp8 (both hosted on Groq). Our Hugging Face Space uses gpt-oss-120b, with the model hosted on Groq, offering a rapid response time for LLM calls.

In a recent development, groq runs open models on its custom‑built LPUs, which are designed for AI inference and optimal for repeated agent inferences required by CUGA's architecture, enabling planning, execution, and validation steps to finish fast. The result is strong cost and performance: open models are ~80-90% cheaper than closed alternatives; Groq's OpenAI-compatible APIs meet production latency needs, and CUGA stays fully configurable across models, providers, and deployment topologies.

Sources indicate that to make agent development even more accessible, CUGA integrates with Langflow, an open-source visual programming interface for building LLM-powered workflows. Its intuitive drag-and-drop interface reduces the barrier to entry for those who prefer low-code solutions.

Starting with Langflow 1.7.0, CUGA ships with its own widget, enabling users to assemble complex, multi-tool agents visually and deploy with a click. Give it a try at langflow.org.

We've rolled out a CUGA demo on Hugging Face Spaces to give you a taste of what's possible. This demo showcases a small CRM system and equips CUGA with 20 preconfigured tools for handling sales related data queries and API interactions through the API Agent. To make experimentation even more powerful, the demo provides access to workspace files, enabling you to use predefined policies.

Give it a try on Hugging Face Spaces and share your feedback!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it has become increasingly challenging to assess whether a model’s reported improvements reflect genuine advances or variations in evaluation conditions, dataset composition, or training data that mirrors benchmark tasks. The NVIDIA Nemotron approach to openness addresses this by publishing transparent and reproducible evaluation recipes that make results independently verifiable.

NVIDIA released Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with an explicitly open evaluation approach to make that distinction clear. Alongside the model card, we are publishing the complete evaluation recipe used to generate the results, built with the NVIDIA NeMo Evaluator library, so anyone can rerun the evaluation pipeline, inspect the artifacts, and analyze the outcomes independently.

Industry observers note that we believe that open innovation is the foundation of AI progress. This level of transparency matters because most model evaluations omit critical details. Configs, prompts, harness versions, runtime settings, and logs are often missing or underspecified, and even small differences in these parameters can materially change results. Without a complete recipe, it’s nearly impossible to tell whether a model is genuinely more intelligent or simply optimized for a benchmark.

In a recent development, this blog demonstrates developers exactly how to reproduce the evaluation behind Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B using fully open tools, configurations, and artifacts. You’ll learn how the evaluation was run, why the methodology matters, and how to execute the same end-to-end workflow using the NeMo Evaluator library so you can verify results, compare models consistently, and build transparent evaluation pipelines of your own.

Developers and researchers need evaluation workflows they can rely on, not one-off scripts that behave differently from model to model. NeMo Evaluator provides a unified way to define benchmarks, prompts, configuration, and runtime behavior once, then reuse that methodology across models and releases. This avoids the common scenario where the evaluation setup quietly changes between runs, making comparisons over time difficult or misleading.

Model outputs can vary by inference backend and configuration, so evaluation tools should never be tied to a single inference solution. Locking an evaluation tool to one inference solution would limit its usefulness. NeMo Evaluator avoids this by separating the evaluation pipeline from the inference backend, allowing the same configuration to run against hosted endpoints, local deployments, or third-party providers. This separation enables meaningful comparisons even when you change infrastructure or inference engines.

Recent findings suggest that many evaluation pipelines work once and then break down as the scope expands. NeMo Evaluator is designed to scale from quick, single-benchmark validation to full model card suites and repeated evaluations across multiple models. The launcher, artifact layout, and configuration model support ongoing workflows, not just isolated experiments, so teams can maintain consistent evaluation practices over time.

It has been revealed that transparent evaluation requires more than final scores. Each evaluation run produces structured results and logs by default, making it easy to inspect how scores were computed, understand score calculations, debug unexpected behavior, and conduct deeper analysis. Each component of the evaluation is captured and reproducible.

It has been revealed that by releasing Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B with its full evaluation recipe, NVIDIA is providing a reference methodology that the community can run, inspect, and build upon. Using the same configuration and tools brings consistency to how benchmarks are selected, executed, and interpreted, enabling more reliable comparisons across models, providers, and releases.

Open evaluation means publishing not just the final results, but the full methodology behind them, so benchmarks are run consistently, and results can be compared meaningfully over time. For Nemotron 3 Nano 30B A3B, this includes open‑source tooling, transparent configurations, and reproducible artifacts that anyone can run end‑to‑end.

NeMo Evaluator is an open-source library designed for robust, reproducible, and scalable evaluation of generative models. Instead of introducing yet another standalone benchmark runner, it acts as a unifying orchestration layer that brings multiple evaluation harnesses under a single, consistent interface.

It has been revealed that under this architecture, NeMo Evaluator integrates and coordinates hundreds of benchmarks from many widely used evaluation harnesses, including NeMo Skills for Nemotron instruction-following, tool use, and agentic evaluations, as well as the LM Evaluation Harness for base model and pre-training benchmarks, and many more (full benchmark catalog). Each harness retains its native logic, datasets, and scoring semantics, while NeMo Evaluator standardizes how they are configured, executed, and logged.

This provides two practical advantages: teams can run diverse benchmark categories using a single configuration without rewriting custom evaluation scripts, and results from different harnesses are stored and inspected in a consistent, predictable way, even when the underlying tasks differ. The same orchestration framework used internally by NVIDIA’s Nemotron research and model‑evaluation teams is now available to the community, enabling developers to run heterogeneous, multi‑harness evaluations through a shared, auditable workflow.

This structure makes it possible to understand not only the final scores, but also how those scores were produced and to perform deeper analysis of model behavior.

Modern evaluation introduces several sources of non‑determinism: decoding settings, repeated trials, judge‑based scoring, parallel execution, and differences in serving infrastructure. The evaluation recipe released alongside Nemotron 3 Nano represents a meaningful step toward a more transparent and reliable approach to open-model evaluation. We are moving away from evaluation as a collection of bespoke, "black box" scripts, and towards a defined system where benchmark selection, prompts, and execution semantics are encoded into a transparent workflow.

In a recent development, for developers and researchers, this transparency changes what it means to share results. A score is only as trustworthy as the methodology behind it and making that methodology public is what enables the community to verify claims, compare models fairly, and continue building on shared foundations. With open evaluation configurations, open artifacts, and open tooling, Nemotron 3 Nano demonstrates what that commitment to openness looks like in practice.

NeMo Evaluator supports this shift by providing a consistent benchmarking methodology across models, releases, and inference environments. The objective isn’t identical numbers on every run; it’s confidence in an evaluation methodology that is explicit, inspectable, and repeatable. And for organizations that need automated or large‑scale evaluation pipelines, a separate microservice offering provides an enterprise‑ready NeMo Evaluator microservice built on the same evaluation principles.
